title: When Intractable Conflicts Require Separation, Not Repair
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that some workplace conflicts become so self-reinforcing that continued interdependence between the parties only deepens the damage, making separation the wiser path rather than continued attempts at repair. It explains how ordinary conflict can cross a threshold into intractability, locking people into cycles of mistrust that negotiation cannot unwind. The piece pushes back on the common leadership instinct to view separation as a failure or abdication, framing it instead as a deliberate tool that removes the reliance keeping the conflict alive. It closes with the idea that distance, not permanent severance, is often what makes eventual reconciliation possible.
points: Interdependence raises the stakes of relationships, intensifying both cooperation and conflict.
Some conflicts cross a threshold into intractability, becoming self-reinforcing cycles that ordinary negotiation cannot resolve.
Continued interdependence in an intractable conflict deepens the wound rather than allowing progress.
Leaders often avoid separation because they see it as defeatist or impractical, letting conflicts fester too long.
Separation doesn't require permanent severance, only enough distance to break the escalatory cycle.
quotes: Some conflicts can’t be resolved or managed, at least not in the short run.
When people or groups rely on each other to attain goals or outcomes, they are said to be interdependent.
Once it crosses this threshold, the parties become locked into self-reinforcing cycles of mistrust, moral condemnation, and hostility that ordinary negotiation cannot unwind.
Separation often works because it removes the reliance that keeps the disagreement alive and escalating.
They wisely believe that sometimes the fastest way back together is to first let go.
